claims.claim: A single-question exit ticket asking each child to describe (orally or by pointing at blocks) what their MakeCode program does gives a low-friction formative read on whether the input→output concept landed, fitting the last 5 min of a 45-60 min session.

Demo-based checks—each pair holds up their micro:bit running the program so the teacher can see the LED or animation respond—are the most authentic lightweight assessment for physical-computing lessons and avoid written work entirely.
Peer-share prompts (turn-and-talk: 'show your partner one block and explain what it does') use peer instruction to surface misconceptions about event/loop blocks without any grading.
A prediction prompt before flashing—'what will the LEDs show when I press button A?'—is a quick formative check of mental-model building for block sequencing.
For a first session, formative assessment should be observational/binary (did it run? can they explain it?) rather than scored, keeping cognitive load on the making, not the testing.
A share-circle where each child shows one thing they made doubles as motivation and a teacher walk-around coverage check, especially effective as the capstone check for L1-s6.
